template_params.session: user_pseudo_id with ga_session_id, from session_start events

prompt: Aoife, the performance marketing manager, is choosing which channels' landing pages to rework first and asks how often each channel's sessions in November 2025 were engaged, from the GA4 export. A channel is the visitor's first-touch medium, the medium in traffic_source, which is the same on every event of a visitor, so a returning visitor's later sessions count under the medium that first brought the visitor in; direct traffic shows as (none). Take the session_start events on the Dublin days from 1 to 30 November 2025, by event_date. A session is one user_pseudo_id with one ga_session_id, counted once; a session_start with no user_pseudo_id or no ga_session_id comes from a visitor who denied consent and belongs to no session you can count, so leave it out, and the events Mailvora's server sends belong to no session either. A session is engaged when the session_engaged parameter of its session_start event is the text '1'. Return one row for each first-touch medium with at least one session, with four columns in this order: first_touch_medium; sessions; engaged_sessions, the sessions that are engaged; and engaged_pct, 100 times engaged_sessions divided by sessions, rounded to 1 decimal. Sort by first_touch_medium from A to Z.
hints: Next, read ga_session_id and session_engaged out of each session_start event's parameters, one value per event.
Count a session as the pair of user_pseudo_id and ga_session_id, leaving out a start where either is missing, then group by the medium in traffic_source.
why_this_works: A session is the pair of visitor and session ID, so two visitors who start in the same second stay two sessions, and session_engaged is read as the text it is.
